name: Ataxia with Oculomotor Apraxia Type 1
aliases: Early-onset ataxia with oculomotor apraxia and hypoalbuminaemia

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive early-onset cerebellar ataxia caused by biallelic APTX mutations affecting aprataxin, an enzyme that resolves abortive intermediates during DNA single-strand break repair.
Onset is usually in early childhood with progressive gait ataxia, followed by oculomotor apraxia and a severe axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy.
Oculomotor apraxia manifests as difficulty initiating voluntary horizontal saccades with compensatory head thrusts, and may evolve towards limitation of gaze.
Extrapyramidal features, particularly chorea and choreoathetosis, are often prominent early and may later be overshadowed by neuropathy, areflexia and distal amyotrophy.
A characteristic biochemical signature of hypoalbuminaemia and hypercholesterolaemia develops as the disease progresses.
Serum alpha-fetoprotein is normal or only mildly raised, an important discriminator from ataxia with oculomotor apraxia type 2 and from ataxia-telangiectasia.
There is no cutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity or increased malignancy risk, distinguishing it from ataxia-telangiectasia.
Brain imaging shows cerebellar atrophy, particularly of the vermis, and cognition may be variably affected over time.
reference.pathophysiology: AOA1 results from loss-of-function variants in APTX, encoding aprataxin, a nuclear protein that participates in single-strand break repair by removing adenosine monophosphate groups from the 5' ends of DNA left by abortive ligation reactions. Without functional aprataxin these adenylated, blocked ends accumulate and unrepaired single-strand breaks persist, imposing chronic genotoxic stress on long-lived, non-dividing cells. Cerebellar Purkinje neurons and dorsal root ganglion neurons appear especially vulnerable, producing the combination of cerebellar cortical degeneration and a severe sensorimotor axonal neuropathy that defines the disorder. The associated hypoalbuminaemia and hypercholesterolaemia are consistent metabolic accompaniments whose precise mechanistic link to defective DNA repair remains incompletely understood, but they serve as reproducible biochemical markers that support the clinical diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Abetalipoproteinaemia and vitamin E deficiency as treatable mimics
Other early-onset autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias
additionalInvestigations: Serum albumin and fasting lipid profile
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
Brain MRI assessing cerebellar and vermian atrophy
Targeted APTX sequencing or a recessive ataxia gene panel
Clinical saccade assessment or oculography for oculomotor apraxia
Serial monitoring of albumin and cholesterol over time
redFlags: Rapidly progressive loss of independent ambulation
New bulbar symptoms with swallowing difficulty and aspiration risk
Nutritional compromise associated with marked hypoalbuminaemia
Progressive scoliosis or contractures threatening respiratory function
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive, with most affected individuals becoming wheelchair-dependent within one to two decades of onset, although lifespan is often relatively preserved. Cognitive function is variably affected and neuropathy tends to dominate the later disability.
pitfalls: Attributing prominent early chorea to a primary movement disorder and missing the underlying recessive ataxia.
Treating a normal alpha-fetoprotein as reassurance against a DNA-repair ataxia, when it is precisely the feature that points towards AOA1 rather than AOA2 or ataxia-telangiectasia.
Pursuing hepatic or renal causes for hypoalbuminaemia rather than recognising it as a diagnostic clue.
Confusing AOA1 with ataxia-telangiectasia and thereby mismanaging radiosensitivity or malignancy-surveillance considerations.
management: Supportive neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy, plus mobility aids and wheelchair provision as ambulation is lost
Management of the axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with orthoses, foot care and neuropathic-pain treatment, and symptomatic treatment of chorea and other extrapyramidal features
Monitoring and management of the associated hypercholesterolaemia and hypoalbuminaemia, with lipid-lowering therapy where indicated
Occupational and visual adaptation strategies for oculomotor apraxia
Multidisciplinary neurology follow-up tracking progressive disability
Genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive APTX-related disorder
